sources.titre: Do goldfish really only have a 3 second memory?
sources.extrait: The prevalent myth that goldfish only have a three-second memory does goldfish a great disservice […] In fact, goldfish can retain memories for at least three months, can be trained, and can also tell the time.

sources.titre: Do fish really have a 3 second memory?
sources.extrait: In fact, most fish - including goldfish - are more than capable of performing pretty good feats of learning and memory […] And these memories last for months, not minutes. […] According to a study by animal psychologists at Plymouth University, goldfish can even tell the time.

sources.titre: Do goldfish really have a 3-second memory?
sources.extrait: However, this is a complete myth that, despite its lack of scientific backing, has spread widely […] In reality, goldfish (Carassius auratus) have much longer memories — spanning weeks, months and even years, Brown said.

panneaux.texte: Deux cœurs poussent le sang dans les branchies, où il se charge en oxygène.
Le troisième envoie ce sang riche en oxygène vers le reste du corps.
panneaux.sous_texte: Et son sang est bleu, à cause du cuivre.

sources.titre: How many hearts does an octopus have?
sources.extrait: It turns out that an octopus has three hearts […] It pumps oxygenated blood around the body, but not to the gills. […] Each branchial heart's job is to pump blood through the gill it is attached to.

sources.editeur: Smithsonian Magazine (Rachel Nuwer, mis à jour en mars 2024)
sources.extrait: Two of the hearts work exclusively to move blood past the animal’s gills, where it releases carbon dioxide and gains oxygen. Then, the third heart circulates that oxygen-rich blood to the organs and muscles […] the copper in octopus blood makes it appear blue.

sources.titre: Why Are Flamingos Pink? And Other Flamingo Facts
sources.extrait: Flamingos really are what they eat. Many plants produce natural red, yellow or orange pigments, called carotenoids. As a flamingo dines on algae and brine shrimp, its body metabolizes the pigments — turning its feathers pink. […] Flamingo chicks hatch with white-gray, downy feathers and straight bills. It takes several years for them to acquire their signature pink color

The bird's digestive system extracts pigment from carotenoid-containing food and it eventually dissolves in fats. The fats are then deposited in new feathers as they grow, and the flamingo's color slowly shifts to pink. […] its new feathers would begin grow in with a much more pale shade.
